name: Gregory of Nyssa

seo.title: St Gregory of Nyssa: universal salvation, Macrina and feast days
seo.description: Who Gregory of Nyssa was, in plain words: Basil's brother, Macrina's deathbed, his hope that all will be saved, his feast days and his words.

band.lede: Basil's younger brother. He wrote the Life of his sister Macrina, and he hoped God would one day heal everyone.

card.line: Basil's younger brother. He wrote the Life of his sister Macrina, and he hoped God would one day heal everyone.

who: Gregory was Basil the Great's younger brother, and one of the three Cappadocian Fathers. He taught rhetoric before Basil made him bishop of Nyssa, a small Cappadocian town, in 372. An Arian emperor drove him out for two years. He was a leader at the Council of Constantinople in 381. He hoped that in the end God would heal everyone.

roles.name: Teacher of rhetoric
roles.line: Scolded for it by a friend

roles.name: Theologian
roles.line: A leader at the council of 381

lines: Over a road like a precipice
No seat, no greeting, no meal

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 335, most likely at Caesarea in Cappadocia, today **Kayseri in Turkey**. The year and the place are not certain.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In a large Christian family in Cappadocia and Pontus. His father was a famous rhetorician, and he died young. His mother Emmelia and his sister Macrina taught him the faith. His brother Basil was his teacher, “our common father and teacher”.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: After 394, probably **about 395**. No one recorded where or how. Where he was buried is not known.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Gregory Nyssen**, in older English. **Gregorius Nyssenus**, in Latin. Later writers called him **the Father of Fathers** and **the Star of Nyssa**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics and Orthodox. Anglicans and Lutherans keep his day too.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In the fresco at the top of this page, a bishop with a long dark beard, in a white vestment covered with dark crosses, holding a scroll. In the engraving below, a Western bishop with a crozier and a book.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: A great deal. The Great Catechism, the Life of Macrina, the Life of Moses, books against Eunomius, sermons and letters.

portrait.alt: An engraving of Gregory of Nyssa as a bearded Western bishop in a flowing cope, holding a crozier and a clasped book, looking down
portrait.credit: S. Gregorius Nyssenus, engraved by Francesco Bartolozzi after Domenichino. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Francesco Bartolozzi
portrait.caption: An engraving by Francesco Bartolozzi (1727 to 1815), after a painting by Domenichino. Here he is a Western bishop, with a crozier and a clasped book. Public domain.

west.text: **Catholic**, in the Roman Martyrology of 2004. He has no memorial in the General Roman Calendar. Also Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod**, with Basil and Gregory Nazianzen.
**Episcopal Church**. Also the **1916 Roman Martyrology**, which kept him on this day.
**ELCA**, with Basil, Gregory Nazianzen and Macrina.
**Church of England**, with his sister Macrina. A Lesser Festival.

east.text: **Russian Church**. This is 10 January on the old calendar.

feasts.note: Why so many dates? The East keeps him on 10 January. The West long kept him on 9 March, as the 1916 Martyrology did. The Roman Martyrology of 2004 now has him on 10 January too. Churches on the old calendar keep 10 January 13 days later, on 23 January.

traits.title: too simple for politics
traits.text: Basil doubted he should be sent to Rome on church business. His brother was “quite inexperienced in ecclesiastical affairs”, he wrote. But he added that Gregory was a man “to whom anything like mean servility is unknown”.

traits.title: quick to tears
traits.text: When Basil died, he went to Macrina, looking “for one who could feel it equally, to mingle my tears with”. When she died, he writes, “neglecting my duties, I gave myself up to lamentation”. Coming home to Nyssa, he “rejoiced and wept with my people”.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection; Life of Macrina; Letter 3

traits.title: stung by slights, and honest about it
traits.text: He rode fifteen miles over a road “like a precipice” to make peace with a bishop who disliked him. He waited outside in the heat till noon, and inside he got no seat and no greeting. He admits the fight within him: “the one, of anger at the insult caused by pride, the other prompting to appease the rising storm”. He also let Flavian know he was that bishop's equal “in education for instance, or in birth … or in theology”.

traits.title: in love with the world's beauty
traits.text: Writing from a friend's country house by the river Halys, he said the famous beauty spots of the poets could not match it: “Your Helicon is nothing: the Islands of the Blest are a fable”. Below the house the river “gleams like a golden ribbon through their deep purple”.

traits.title: able to laugh at himself
traits.text: Writing to a young lover of the classics, he opened with Homer instead of the Bible, since that was what the young man read. Then he apologised for rambling: “for garrulity is just as characteristic of old age as to be blear-eyed, or for the limbs to fail”.

cite.text: Letter 8, to a student of the classics

said.lede: The people closest to him did not flatter him. His brother scolded him and his sister corrected him. His friend Gregory Nazianzen kept him going.

quotes.q: How can I lay hold of you satisfactorily, with all your simplicity? Tell me; who ever falls a third time into the same nets?
quotes.who: Basil, his brother, when a third doubtful letter came

quotes.q: Let him be a bishop, not deriving dignity from his see, but conferring dignity on his see by himself.
quotes.who: Basil, to a friend surprised that he made his brother bishop of so small a town

cite.text: Basil, Letter 98, to Eusebius of Samosata

quotes.q: But you are renowned in cities and peoples and nations. Churches summon you as an ally and director, and do you not see the grace of God in it all?
quotes.who: Macrina, his sister, on the day before she died, when he complained of his troubles

quotes.q: …you who are the common prop of the whole Church.
quotes.who: Gregory Nazianzen, writing to him in exile

quotes.q: …seeing his character in you as in a bright and shining mirror, I may think myself to possess him also!

moments.title: The rhetoric teacher
moments.text: He read the Scriptures to the people in church. Then he gave it up to teach rhetoric, like his father. His friend Gregory Nazianzen wrote to scold him. He said Gregory had hung up the holy books “over the chimney, as men do in winter with rudders and hoes”. People were whispering that Gregory “preferred to be called a Professor of Rhetoric rather than of Christianity”.

cite.text: Gregory Nazianzen, a letter to Gregory of Nyssa

moments.title: The forged letter
moments.text: Basil had fallen out with their uncle, a bishop. To make peace, Gregory forged a letter from the uncle. Basil was delighted and showed it round, until the uncle said he never wrote it. Basil was furious: “You forged one letter, and brought it me as though it came from our right reverend uncle the bishop, trying to deceive me, I have no idea why.” The quarrel was mended in the end. Basil wrote to the uncle: “Formerly I was glad to see my brother. Why not, since he is my brother and such a brother?”

cite.text: Basil, Letters 58 and 60; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, introduction

moments.title: Made bishop
moments.text: Basil wanted allies against the Arians, so he made his brother bishop of Nyssa, a small town, over his protests. A friend was surprised he chose such an obscure place. Basil said his brother deserved “the whole Church under the sun gathered into one place”. Since he could not have that, he would bring honour to little Nyssa.

cite.text: Basil, Letter 98, to Eusebius of Samosata; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, introduction

moments.title: Arrested, and driven out
moments.text: A governor serving the Arian emperor Valens took up charges against him: wasting church money, and an irregular election. Soldiers took him away. On the road he fell ill with his “old kidney complaint”, and he escaped to a safe place. A synod at Nyssa deposed him in 376, and he wandered from town to town until Valens died. Gregory Nazianzen once cheered him about his travels. They were like the planets, he wrote, “whose very wandering is harmonious”.

cite.text: Basil, Letter 225; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910; Gregory Nazianzen, Letter 81

moments.title: Home again
moments.text: When he came home, the villages along the river road were full of people weeping for joy. At his church the crowd pressed so close that he nearly fainted. Then he saw “a stream of fire flowing into the church”. It was the choir of consecrated virgins, marching in with torches. He wrote to a friend the moment the prayers were done, before he even had a drink.

moments.title: His sister's deathbed
moments.text: Nine months after Basil died, Gregory went to see Macrina. He found her dying of fever, lying on boards on the floor. When he poured out his troubles, she scolded him: “Will you not cease to be insensible to the divine blessings? Will you not remedy the ingratitude of your soul?” She died the next evening, praying. He laid her in their parents' grave, and “threw myself on the grave and embraced the dust”. Their last talks became his book On the Soul and the Resurrection.

moments.title: An unimpressed pilgrim
moments.text: A council sent him to set the churches of Arabia in order, and he went on to Jerusalem. The emperor let him travel by the state post. His wagon “was, in fact, as good as a church or monastery to us”, he said. Jerusalem shocked him: theft, adultery and murder were everywhere. Later he told a friend that pilgrimage brings no one nearer to God. Cappadocia had more altars: “One could hardly count so many in all the rest of the world.”

moments.title: The great council
moments.text: He was one of the 150 bishops at the Council of Constantinople. He preached at the funeral of Meletius of Antioch, the council's first president. Afterwards the emperor Theodosius named the bishops whose communion marked the true faith. For the cities of Pontus he named three: Helladius of Caesarea, Otreius of Melitene, and Gregory.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 7, chapter 9; Socrates, Book 5, chapter 8

extras.title: Wonders he wrote down
extras.lede: No early writer says Gregory worked a miracle himself. But he wrote wonders down. Two happened to him. The rest are his sister Macrina's, as he heard them at her death.

items.title: The shining relics
items.text: On his way to Macrina, he dreamed three times in one night that he carried martyrs' relics, too bright to look at. At her deathbed he understood: the relics were his sister. After she died, even in a dark robe, rays seemed to shine from her.
items.quote: I seemed to be carrying martyrs' relics in my hands; a light came from them, such as comes from a clear mirror when it is put facing the sun, so that my eyes were blinded by the brilliance of the rays.

items.title: The healed tumour
items.text: Years before, Macrina had a tumour on her breast. Her mother begged her to see a doctor, since medicine “was sent from God for the saving of men”. Macrina would not let a stranger see her body. She prayed all night, weeping, and asked her mother to make the sign of the cross on the place. After her death, the widow Vestiana showed Gregory the small scar.
items.quote: But when the mother put her hand within her bosom, to make the sign of the cross on the part, the sign worked and the tumour disappeared.

items.title: The soldier's daughter
items.text: On the road home, a soldier who was a relative told Gregory a story. Macrina had kissed his little girl's diseased eye and promised them a medicine. They forgot to take it. As someone ran back for it, the child's mother saw the eye was healed, and cried out:
items.quote: She has indeed given her the true drug which cures disease; it is the healing that comes from prayer.

items.title: The grain that did not run out
items.text: In a famine, Macrina gave grain to the hungry all the time, and it never got less. Gregory mentions it only in passing. He also leaves out healings, demons cast out and true predictions.
items.quote: the corn for the relief of need, though constantly distributed, suffered no perceptible diminution

items.title: The storm that held off
items.text: On the road home to Nyssa, a great storm gathered all round them, with thunder and lightning. They reached shelter dry, and only then did the rain pour down. Three or four hours later it stopped, and they went on. Gregory calls it “a manifest token of His loving kindness”.
items.quote: and yet we, like the Israelites of old in their miraculous passage of the Red Sea, though surrounded on all sides by rain, arrived unwetted at Vestena.

items.title: He expected doubt
items.text: Gregory says he left most of her wonders out, because people would not believe them.
items.quote: For most men judge what is credible in the way of a tale by the measure of their own experience. But what exceeds the capacity of the hearer, men receive with insult and suspicion of falsehood, as remote from truth.

extras.title: His hope that all will be saved
extras.lede: Gregory hoped that in the end God would heal everyone. It is the hardest question about him, so here it is in his own words and in his critics'.

items.title: What he wrote
items.text: Gregory says God's fire works like a gold refiner's. It burns the dross away, and the pain heals. In the end evil will be gone. Even the devil, “the introducer of evil himself”, will be healed. Then all creation will give thanks together.
items.quote: …when there has been a restoration of those who are now lying in Sin to their primal state, a harmony of thanksgiving will arise from all creation.

items.title: Not his only word
items.text: The 1893 English edition of his works notes that elsewhere he speaks of eternal fire for the merciless rich. There, it says, “the language of Scripture as to future punishment is used without any modification”. One example is his second sermon On Loving the Poor. It adds that such sermons urge people on, so they weigh less as evidence.

cite.text: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, introduction, chapter 3

items.title: What the critics said
items.text: In the sixth century, a set of anathemas condemned Origen's restoration of all, which rested on his belief that souls exist before birth. They do not name Gregory. Whether the council of 553 itself passed them is still argued. Gregory did not share that belief about souls, says the New Catholic Encyclopedia, but he did teach the restoration of all.
items.quote: If anyone asserts the fabulous pre-existence of souls, and shall assert the monstrous restoration which follows from it: let him be anathema.

cite.text: The Anathemas against Origen, the first

items.title: Never condemned
items.text: No council condemned him by name. The emperor's letter read at the council of 553 lists him among the holy Fathers it follows. The Council in Trullo, in 692, took his canons into church law.
items.quote: in every way follow the holy Fathers, Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose

cite.text: Fifth Ecumenical Council, Session 1, the emperor's letter; Council in Trullo, canon 2

items.title: Were his books changed?
items.text: In the eighth century Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, argued that Origen's followers had slipped these ideas into Gregory's books. His book is lost. The 1893 English edition doubts it: the ideas are “portions of the very groundwork of his own theology”. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 calls the theory “useless and gratuitous”.

cite.text: Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 233; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910

words.note: Gregory wrote a great deal. These lines are from Moore and Wilson's translation of 1893. Some of his best-known books, like the Life of Moses, have no public-domain English translation, so they are not quoted here.

feature.q: Change of place does not effect any drawing nearer unto God, but wherever thou mayest be, God will come to thee, if the chambers of thy soul be found of such a sort that He can dwell in thee and walk in thee.
feature.ctx: To a friend who asked whether monks should travel to Jerusalem.

quotes.q: Counsel the brethren to be absent from the body to go to our Lord, rather than to be absent from Cappadocia to go to Palestine.
quotes.who: The same letter, a little later.

quotes.q: The soul immediately shows its royal and exalted character, far removed as it is from the lowliness of private station, in that it owns no lord, and is self-governed, swayed autocratically by its own will.
quotes.who: On why every human being is made to be royal.

cite.text: On the Making of Man, chapter 4

quotes.q: They therefore do not understand that all virtue is found in moderation, and that any declension to either side of it becomes a vice.
quotes.who: On those who called marriage, and God's good gifts, foul.

quotes.q: I answered rather audaciously, and without due consideration of what I said, for my passionate grief had not yet given me back my judgment.
quotes.who: Arguing with his dying sister about death, while he still grieved for Basil.

cite.text: On the Soul and the Resurrection, the opening

myths.claim: He said, *Concepts create idols; only wonder grasps anything.*
myths.truth: We could not find this sentence in any of his works we could read. Quote sites give it in several wordings, which is the mark of a modern summary. It is often traced to his Life of Moses, which has no public-domain English translation.

cite.text: His works in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, searched

myths.claim: He forged three letters from his uncle.
myths.truth: Basil says Gregory forged one. A second came by Gregory's servant, and it was not from the uncle either. Then a third came. But Basil never says Gregory wrote them.

myths.claim: He wrote the clauses added to the Nicene Creed in 381.
myths.truth: Some say so, and the OCA's life of him agrees. But the 1893 English edition of his works calls it “very doubtful”.

cite.text: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, introduction, chapter 1; OCA

myths.truth: No one knows. Gregory Nazianzen's letter on her death calls her “truly consort of a priest”, which some read as his wife. The same letter calls her “your holy and blessed sister”, and the OCA honours her as his sister. He may have married, but that too is argued.

myths.claim: The Seventh Ecumenical Council, in 787, named him the Father of Fathers.
myths.truth: We could not trace this to any council text. The 1893 English edition says only that “some did not hesitate” to call him that. Later writers did.

cite.text: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, introduction, chapter 1

myths.claim: His joke about Constantinople, where the baker and the bath attendant argue about the Trinity, in his own words.
myths.truth: The story is his, from a sermon he preached at Constantinople. But it has no public-domain English translation. Every English version is a paraphrase, and the words change from book to book.

stood.lede: Each line is from his own writings. The line on being alone is Ecclesiastes, which he quotes, in New Advent's lightly modernised text.

circle.name: Basil the Great
circle.text: His older brother and teacher, “our common father and teacher”. Basil made him a bishop, and scolded him often.

cite.text: On the Making of Man; Basil, Letters 58 and 215

circle.name: Macrina
circle.text: His oldest sister, who taught the whole family. He wrote her Life, and made her the teacher in his dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection.

cite.text: Life of Macrina; On the Soul and the Resurrection

circle.name: Gregory Nazianzen
circle.text: Basil's friend and fellow worker. He scolded Gregory for teaching rhetoric, then wrote to comfort him in exile.

cite.text: Gregory Nazianzen, Letters; Theodoret, Book 4, chapter 27

circle.name: Peter of Sebaste
circle.text: The youngest brother, raised by Macrina, and later a bishop himself. Gregory wrote On the Making of Man for him.

cite.text: Life of Macrina; On the Making of Man

circle.name: Naucratius
circle.text: A brother who gave up a brilliant start as a speaker to live alone by the river Iris. He fed poor old men there, and died suddenly on one of his trips to feed them.

circle.name: Helladius
circle.text: Basil's successor at Caesarea. In 381 the emperor named them side by side. Later Helladius snubbed him, and Gregory complained of it in a long letter.

circle.name: Eunomius
circle.text: The Arian leader who attacked Basil's teaching. Gregory answered him in his long books Against Eunomius.

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: He heard Gregory read his work aloud. Gregory, he wrote, “a few years since read to Gregory Nazianzan and myself a work against Eunomius”.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 128

death.big: No one recorded how he died. The last we hear of him is at a council in Constantinople in 394.
paras: He probably died soon after, about 395. No early source gives the day, the place or the cause.

Basil had said his brother would bring honour to little Nyssa. At that last council, says the 1893 English edition, “Nyssa was ennobled by the name of its bishop”. He was listed between the bishops of the great sees of Caesarea and Iconium.
He left no deathbed story of his own. But he wrote down his sister's, with her last prayer. These are her words, not his.

items.k: Macrina's dying prayer, as he wrote it down
items.q: Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death. Thou hast made the end of this life the beginning to us of true life. Thou for a season restest our bodies in sleep and awakest them again at the last trump.
items.ctx: She prayed facing east, as the sun went down.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics and Orthodox count him a saint, and Anglicans and Lutherans keep his day. He was never condemned, though his hope that all will be saved has troubled some.

churches.note: 10 January (23 January for the Russian Church)
Church of England 19 July, Episcopal Church 9 March

paras: The Roman Martyrology of 1916 remembered him in one line:

quotes.q: At Nyssa, the demise of St. Gregory, bishop, brother of blessed Basil the Great, whose life and erudition have rendered him illustrious.
quotes.who: The Roman Martyrology, 1916 edition, for 9 March
